speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEFENCE SERVICES'-PROTECTION OF RIGHTS OF PERSONNEL TRANSFERRING FROM ONE ARMED SERVICE TO ANOTHER
speechtext:
I should like to table copies, in
English and in French, of an order in council passed yesterday under the Emergency Powers Act to provide that warrant officers, non-commissioned officers or men who are granted commissions, who leave one of the services for the purpose of joining another of the services, and therefore under the text of the Defence Services Pension Act become discharged, will not have their defence pensions interfered with by their so doing.
There are about 170 whom it is necessary to promote to special temporary commissions for the proper functioning of this special brigade which is being organized. Under the act the taking of those temporary special commissions would terminate their right under the Defence Services Pension Act; their contributions would have to be returned to them, and that would involve complications when their temporary commissions expire.
This is one of the provisions to be made in the bill with respect to which there is a resolution on the order paper as No. 11. We had hoped that that bill would be reached and passed in time to take care of this, but we are told that the delay in commissioning these 170 men is a serious inconvenience in the organization of the special force. For that reason, because of the urgency of the matter and the fact that it may be a couple of weeks before this statute could be passed and receive royal assent, the order in council has been passed so the commissioning may be done immediately.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER MONDAY, JUNE 11
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel sure that
at this stage of the session there will be a tendency on the part of hon. members to support this motion, which has become customary at this time of the year. But I suggest that this is an appropriate occasion to review what has happened during the present session which calls for a motion of this kind, at this time, particularly in relation to the announcement made a few days ago that it is the intention to adjourn the present session until October and then, having met, prorogue for the purpose of having a second session this year.
When the announcement was made a few days ago I urged the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to reconsider his statement- and it must be recalled that it was simply an announcement at that time. I did so in view of the fact that in the opinion of a number of members the legislation now before the house should be dealt with before this house rises. The explanation was given that it was desirable to defer consideration of the old age pension legislation until later this year. When that announcement was made, I said, and I repeat today, that I believe there are many strong reasons why that legislation should be dealt with before this house rises even for adjournment.
The passing of the old age pension legislation is not going to take very long. The members of this house have already indicated their desire to proceed with it as rapidly as possible. That was indicated in statements made earlier in the session. It was also indicated very clearly by the manner in which this house adopted, without debate and with every sign of unanimous approval, the request to Westminster for an amendment to the British North America Act.
[Mr. St. Laurent.)

Since the legislation dealing with universal pensions at seventy and over and the special legislation dealing with pensions from sixty-five to sixty-nine inclusive has met with agreement on the part of members of this house, I feel certain, and I am sure there is confidence in the minds of hon. members, that such legislation would be facilitated in every way. I can see no reason why that legislation should not be dealt with in one day, or in two days at the very outside. Therefore I see no reason why that legislation should not be dealt with before we rise for the summer.
I am not overlooking the explanation by the Prime Minister that the same plan might not be proposed were it not for the fact that other legislation requires consideration. He indicated that it was desirable to carry into effect by legislation those recommendations in the report of the transportation commission which the government is prepared to accept, and also indicated that it might be desirable this year to introduce legislation to implement some of the recommendations of the Massey commission.
So far as the recommendations of the transport commission are concerned, I concede that there will certainly not be complete unanimity in regard to the statutory interpretation of those recommendations. The same attitude will probably not be demonstrated as will be found when we are dealing with the recommendations in connection with the old age pension legislation. Nevertheless I am sure that if there is sufficient advance notice of what the legislation is intended to be, the members of this house will deal promptly and with very clear thought as to what they wish to have enacted into law when that legislation comes forward. That would not take very long, provided that hon. members have an opportunity in advance to consider the legislation. If the house is only adjourned for the summer, then it is possible, by agreement, to provide copies of the proposed legislation to hon. members and they would have a chance to consider it before we return here to examine it in the ordinary way in the house.
So far as the Massey commission report is concerned, I think that hon. members who have already read the report, or even have merely glanced through it, will realize that most of the recommendations are such that it will take some time to implement them. In any event, there are certain specific recommendations, one with regard to grants to universities and other specialized branches of education, and another with regard to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which

obviously call for consideration, either within the next few days or at any rate certainly by the beginning of next year.
So far as grants to universities are concerned, I submit that all that the Massey report has done is to confirm the opinion that has been expressed here over and over again, that grants should be made to assist the universities without delay, if our higher education is not to suffer. That being so-

speechtext:
I have placed before the house certain reasons why I believe the business of the house can be so facilitated as not to require a second session of parliament, where we would have a new speech from the throne and an extended debate, with time consumed in discussing matters which could well await the beginning of a regular session at the first of next year.
I come now to the necessity for a motion of this kind, a necessity which presents itself year after year. I know that members of the government do not welcome a statement along these lines, because it has been made before. The reason why we are going to be asked to sit at eleven o'clock every day and to sit every night-we are not opposing it, because we face a situation which has been forced upon us-is that there has been no direction of the business of this house from the day the house met at the beginning of this year. There has been no planning of the debates of this house. We have estimates brought up, they continue for a short time in debate, then that is stopped and they are revived some time later when a completely new debate starts. At the present time there are several departments which have been called, have been debated, then have been debated again after a short time, and will be brought before the house again.
I am quite prepared to concede that it has never been the practice in this house to follow the practice with regard to agreed schedule of debate which has been accepted at Westminster. One reason why we do not even approximate anything of that kind, one reason why members have no way of knowing in advance when any debate is to come forward, is that there is no attempt to plan in advance when important debates will
Business of the House come on. At Westminster-and, after all, we have patterned our course largely on their practice-they know a week or two weeks in advance when a debate is going to take place on any subject of major importance. The members are then able to plan their time accordingly. Members of this house certainly have demonstrated the fact that it is necessary for them to be away on a number of occasions, on duties that undoubtedly are connected with their service here; but when it is necessary for them to be away from the house on those duties it is also desirable that they be able to plan such other appointments with some knowledge of when debates will take place.
We could have disposed of all the business of this house before this time, and no such motion as this would now be necessary if there were some knowledge of when debates were going to come on. I know that it can easily be said that there are so many speeches made in the debate on the speech from the throne and on the budget, but one reason why many of those speeches are made is that there is a cynical certainty in the minds of many members of this house that the government is going to defer a lot of important items until the last, so that the very inconvenience of members may make it possible to rush through those items.

speechtext: I come to the remarks that were made after the Prime Minister made this announcement a few days ago. I was interested to hear the comment afterwards-and when I say "afterwards", I mean in this house-that this recognized the fact that membership in the House of Commons is a full-time job. It is a full-time job of representation of a constituency. But it was never intended to be a full-time job here in Ottawa; and there is a reason why it should not be. It was never intended that the members of the parliament of this country should be something in the nature of elected civil servants. It was always intended-and that was the genius of our system-that persons elected to parliament who are actively engaged in many activities in this country would be spending a considerable part of the time with the people of their own constituencies, and that during only a part of the year they would be representing their people here in the House of Commons, with the advantage of that intimate and personal contact in their own ridings which is denied if the members are sitting here most of the time. Mr. Speaker, as a member of a group that supported the Prime Minister's contention that another session was necessary this year I cannot sit here, in view of the speech which has just been made, without giving some of the reasons why we supported the arrangement that brings about the motion now before the house.
In my opinion the leader of the opposition was not facing facts in any of the statements that he made. He is well aware of the fact,
3848	HOUSE OF
Business of the House as are other hon. members, that the business now before this house, namely, the committee work, the legislation on the order paper and all of the things that we have to handle, will keep us going night and day perhaps into July, without touching the different pieces of legislation that he mentioned specifically.
While listening to him I thought the matter over, and I think he considered very lightly the reports that have to come before the house sometime in the future. My conviction is that if we deal with all the legislation that he feels we should deal with we would not get it all through and give it the consideration to which it is entitled if we sat here until September. For example, my thinking, on the old age pension problem has led me to believe that it is going to take more than a month or two months to finalize that particular piece of legislation. The legislation dealing with universal pensions at seventy by right and the legislation dealing with the age group sixty-five to sixty-nine will go forward at the same time. Every province in Canada, with the exception of Ontario and Quebec, will have to raise additional funds in order to give effect to that legislation, if they are to accept the proposition that is being put forward by the federal government. What does that mean? It means that it is going to be necessary to have a dominion-provincial conference to determine where the provinces who have not the additional finances necessary to meet the obligation are to get that money. You cannot hold a dominion-provincial conference between now and the end of June, and that is the fact of the matter. That is what has to take place.
Ontario and Quebec may be ready to go ahead with it. Unfortunately, too many people in this house think in terms of their own provinces. In my opinion the old age pension legislation cannot be finalized before the October session. If the leader of the opposition is as anxious as he makes out that the old age pensioners should receive that money with equality as between the provinces, then he will have to agree that the only way to bring it about is to allow sufficient time to do a reasonable job as it affects the country as a whole.
The leader of the opposition mentioned the Turgeon report. It consists of at least 500 pages, and deals with one of the most complicated problems in this country, namely, freight rates. The adoption of that report means that for a long time we will be setting up machinery with regard to freight rates that will affect the economy of this country for a long time to come. It will affect the eastern and western part of the country to


the extent that they will be able to find markets at reasonable freight rates within the rest of the dominion. It is a report that requires a long and detailed examination, and we would not be able to give it that examination if we sat through until September.
It is not good enough merely to glance at this report. Every hon. member has the responsibility of analysing it, of going through the figures and ascertaining for himself how it will affect the people whom he represents in this house.
Then there is the Massey report. It is a very technical report. It suggests the setting of the culture of this country for the next fifty years. It is something we badly need. We have not any at this time.

It is the first time a prime minister of this country has advised members of the House of Commons, well in advance, that he was going to try to clean up the immediate business of the House of Commons that could be cleaned up, as soon as it could be done, and has indicated that a large amount of important legislation that could not be dealt with at this time, and given due consideration, was to be allowed to stand, and that we would be called back here for the purpose of dealing with that legislation.
It is the first time since I have been here that I have known that I am going home and that I can stay there until October, and that I will come back here in October. In my opinion it is a good development; and I think that instead of the criticism, recriminations and accusations based upon assumptions, suspicions and editorials, the Prime Minister should be commended upon his honest approach to this problem.
The monetary aspect of this matter I will not consider. I am not mercenary. I demonstated when I came to the House of Commons that I was prepared to come here for $4,000 a year. I am still working full time for what I am getting, and I will continue to work full time for what I am getting. I do not want to run home and sell any hardware or anything else. I am anxious to stay here, and I am prepared to do so. I am not concerned about the monetary aspect of the matter. I know that perhaps the fellow who wants to run home at the end of June and stay there until next January might be able to make $12,000. But that aspect of it does not [DOT] concern me at all, and I do not think it concerns the people of Canada.
I would point out to the leader of the opposition, on this question of monetary returns, that members of the House of Commons, in terms of business office hours and the hours of industrial workers, are working twelve months in six. There is no other group of individuals in this country that works until eleven o'clock at night. The trade union movement from which I come would scorn the attitude we take in the House of Commons with regard to hours, social conditions and recreation. They do not ask their employees to work for peanuts, and they do not want them to work all night, either. The average trade union leader in this country today is paid twice as much money as the average member of parliament, and he has a full-time expense account. The worker in a mine, a steel plant, or a textile mill does not want to place his representative in such a position that he has to lose sleep and deprive himself of recreation, or stay in

Business of the House a cheap rooming house or a cheap hotel. He wants his representative to have the best.
There is one thing I am sure of, and that is that the people I represent will never say to the government: You are paying that member too much money. The story I have always got from my people is: "How do you get by on it?" That is the attitude they take. And I think that raising this monetary consideration, in a forum such as this, having regard to the position members of the House of Commons occupy, in one of the highest offices in the country that can be given, voluntarily, by the people in the ridings, is small potatoes. It certainly is not supported by the average Canadian citizen.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said on Monday last: "Membership in the House of Commons today is a full-time position." I entirely refute that statement, and I say to the house that if the time ever comes when the house accepts the view that membership is a full-time position you will thereby automatically be closing the doors of public life, of public careers, to a great many people who cannot afford to take the risks and insecurity of public life. What does it mean? It means that the avenue of public

service in the House of Commons will be open only to those who are possessed of independent means-

This is realism. Membership in the House of Commons will be open only to those who are fortunate enough to be so independent financially that they can give twelve months a year full time to their work as members of parliament or to those who have no family responsibilities and can somehow get along on the somewhat meagre amount that is left out of the sessional indemnity after the expenses and cost of keeping up two establishments and the other financial burdens of public office are met. There is nothing that can be more antidemocratic in its conception than anything which will confine public life to people who are on the one hand possessed of independent means and are completely independent of any financial worries, or to those on the other hand who do not have the responsibilities that most of us have, and somehow can eke out an existence on what may be left out of the sessional indemnity.
Sir, the strength of democracy and the strength of this House of Commons is that there are in this house people drawn from all walks of life. Every aspect of Canadian life in every part of the country is represented in the house, and the strength of this House of Commons is to be measured also in terms of the sum total of the experience which 262 members sitting in the house bring to the discharge of their duties. That is the reason why the experience of members in this house, contributed through debates in the house, contributed through discussions in committees, is so vitally important to the functioning of democracy. If the time ever comes when members of parliament are expected to sever themselves entirely from their other callings and take these risks that go with public life, these risks to their whole economic future, then I say to you, sir, that we will have taken a retrograde step, and democracy in this country will pay for it.
What we must do in shaping the course of parliamentary affairs and parliamentary work in the future is to try to see to it that the doors of public life are not closed to people who, having family responsibilities and
Business of the House responsibilities in other respects, are nevertheless capable of making a most valuable contribution to public life in the House of Commons. If you shut off from public service people bearing these responsibilities, then make no mistake about it, democracy will pay the price in Canada.
How do we go about achieving that purpose? Let me say at once that I do not think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) shares the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It is true that the Prime Minister has never sat in the house as a private member, and he does not know from firsthand experience the problems that face private members. Naturally when one becomes a member of the government he gives his full time to his position, and the compensation is at least intended to bear some resemblance to full-time responsibility. But I think the Prime Minister has some knowledge of the difficulties faced by private members in trying to discharge their duties. I think he has an appreciation also of the importance of keeping the doors of public service open to people in all walks of life, regardless of their means.
I want to say this concerning the proposal to hold a second session. There is not one of us who relishes a protracted session into the summer with its heat; nevertheless I say to you, sir, that is preferable to coming back here in the fall to face a session then. Make no mistake about it. Experience cannot fail to be a sure guide. It should teach us that when we come back the debates will be longer than they would have been if we had continued into the summer. Nobody will relish sitting in July. Nevertheless I say that as between these two choices it is the preferable choice.
I go further and I say that, as to the broader problem of making public life, a public career or public service possible for people who have heavy responsibilities to bear outside this house, two sessions a year are no answer. Whether you pay one indemnity or whether you pay two, that is not the way to handle this problem. It is not a question of indemnity. If the problem of being away from home, from family and from other responsibilities for long periods of the year does not create difficulties for the hon. member I am sure it does for most people in this house. If it is a matter of selfinterest to most of us in that we are separated from our families for long periods-


and this applies to members from western Canada and the far east more than to most of us who come from central Canada-then I say there is self-interest in this for every member.
Therefore I say that the way to have the business of this house done without putting additional obstacles in the way of people giving themselves to public service and making a valuable contribution to this country is to so organize the business of the house that it can be done effectively, efficiently and within a proper time.
I said I would not be speaking today if I were not prepared to make some suggestions to that effect, and I do so because I believe the holding of two sessions a year is not the answer to the problem. The answer is to modernize our procedure and expedite our business so it can be done within a reasonable compass of time; and I am convinced that this is possible. I have some suggestions to offer. I do not pretend that these are the only suggestions that can be made, nor do I pretend that they are altogether new.
In the first place, I believe we can contribute greatly toward expediting the work of the house and the better transaction of our business if we revise the hours of sitting. It was common knowledge to those who were in the last house that the then prime minister, the late Mr. Mackenzie King, did not favour the idea of the house meeting earlier than three o'clock, p.m., under ordinary circumstances. It was hoped that when the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) took over he would consider this question of the hours of sitting and try, with the general co-operation of hon. members and the size of the following he has in this house, to introduce some sanity into the hours of sitting. Here we are, sitting from three o'clock in the afternoon until eleven o'clock at night, the most absurd arrangement of hours imaginable. If the house would get down to some reasonable system, like starting at one o'clock in the afternoon and sitting until seven, we would pick up some time on our present total hours of sittings, and would transact a great deal more business than we do under the present hours. Every hon. member knows that by nine-thirty or ten o'clock at night many hon. members are fagged out, and we make relatively little progress in those late hours of sitting. It would also contribute to the health of hon. members; and I am sure that with better health and greater vigour we would do our work better and faster.

Then I think something could be done in regard to some of the specific debates. I believe if we introduced the sort of sanity I have suggested into the hours of sitting, our committees could meet earlier in the morning. At the present time we cannot call a committee meeting before eleven o'clock in the morning because we are sitting so late at night. If we had reasonable hours of sitting we would be able to get our committee work under way at a proper hour in the morning, and more work would be done because we would be fresher.
It seems to me we put the cart before the horse in this matter. At the time of the session when the committees are not sitting, our hours in the house are easiest. But toward the end of the session, when all the committees are sitting, when they not only overlap each other but overlap the sittings of the house, we bring in morning sittings.
It is an impossible situation. The only time there is reason for morning sittings is in the early stages of the session, before we begin the work of the committees. That is when we have long debates such as that on the speech from the throne, which normally takes about three weeks; and the debate on the budget, though perhaps not so much that debate since it comes at a later stage of the session. There is no reason why we could not have morning sittings while the speech from the throne was being debated, because it consists of a number of set speeches. In that way we could pick up perhaps a couple of weeks of the time of the house.
Then I put forward another suggestion which has been put forward before, and I think something must be done to face up to it. It is the question of the use of the committees of this house for the transaction of much of the business that is done in the house at the present time, but which does not need to come before the house and can be done better in a committee. Much of the work done in connection with the estimates consists of trying to elicit information, often on a multitude of small points. That takes a great deal of the time of this house in committee of supply. We would not sacrifice any of our rights as members by referring much of that business to the committees, just as we do in connection with external affairs. We do not deprive any member of the house of his right to express his views on questions of policy which are properly discussed here, but information which is requested on the smaller details is obtained in the committee on external affairs to which the estimates of that department are referred. We save a great
Business of the House deal of the time of the house in that way, and consequently on the subject of external affairs we have a much more comprehensive and infinitely more orderly and constructive debate in the house than would be possible if it were interspersed with inquiries and discussions on a multitude of small details.
The same thing could be done with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would be content on his estimates to make some of his speeches or give some of his explanations to the standing committee on agriculture, which I believe has not met for several years, we could save days of the time of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member quoted my words of the other afternoon, but he entirely misinterpreted them. I know that since 1945 all my autumns but one have been taken up with conferences relating to international and commonwealth affairs. Other members of the house have been called upon to do the same thing. Apart from obligations of that description, the business of this country and the business of a member of parliament is such that unless he gives his entire attention to his job it is difficult to see how he can fulfil the obligations of the position to which he has been elected.
Again let me say that I was not suggesting that members of parliament should sit here twelve months in the year. I think that no one within sound of my voice on that occasion could possibly have put such an interpretation upon my words. speechtext:
-I often wish some of these great orators would get up and try to demonstrate whether they have much intelligence and try to say a few words on their feet rather than sit back sprawled out in their seats and interrupt people who are at least endeavouring to say something on behalf of those hon. members' constituencies as well as their own. There is one man who is frequent in his interruptions, but I have never heard him speak very intelligently on his feet on any occasion in the House of Commons, either for his constituency or for any other constituency across Canada.
This debate has been exceedingly interesting. I am going to try to speak just as a lowly individual member. I quite agree with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) when he says that it will be a sorry day for the House of Commons when we lose the great asset which the people of Canada now possess in having men of diversified occupations, from all walks of life, sitting here


endeavouring to administer the affairs of the people of Canada. That can only be made possible by people attending to whatever vocation they are carrying on in their home constituencies. If it ever becomes necessary for a member of parliament to devote one hundred per cent of his time to the House of Commons, we will no longer have a democracy or a democratic form of government.
All hon. members, with few exceptions, must undoubtedly agree with those words. We cannot have a democratic form of government unless people are in the position that they can seek and obtain information from people of all walks of life, through association in business. But surely the members of this House of Commons are not so antiquated and steeped in tradition that they cannot get together and smarten up the method by which we are endeavouring to carry on the people's business in the House of Commons. Surely we cannot let tradition hold us in such a vise that our own inveterate intelligence and knowledge, gained through bitter experience, will not serve the members of this house of all parties so that they may devise some method of expediting the service that we are trying to render to the people of Canada. I believe that what we have heard today will be of great benefit to all members of the House of Commons and, therefore, will be beneficial to the people of Canada.
I heard one hon. member, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), talk about remuneration. Let us be frank about it. The rising cost of living affects all members of parliament. Members who, through their integrity, their intelligence and their willing-nes to work, are at times able to make more money than are other members of the House of Commons, are justly entitled to whatever money parliament sees fit to pay members of the House of Commons for the service they render to the people, irrespective of their private income from other sources. Undoubtedly the public of Canada should be aware, as most of them are not, of the length of time that a member of parliament devotes to the duties that he is called upon to perform as their representative. A member of parliament's duties are continuous. You talk about sixteen hours a day. The duties of a member of parliament extend over twenty-four hours a day. He is on call twenty-four hours a day. He comes to the House of Commons around nine o'clock in the morning and opens his mail. He attends the afternoon session, and the session closes in the evening at eleven o'clock. He finally wends his way home and arrives there at twelve or twelve-thirty, if he is fortunate.

The people of Canada do not realize exactly what is involved at the present time in the duties of a member of parliament. There are the committee meetings. They do not speak of this, but members of parliament are on call all the time. Men and women call a member of parliament when he is in his own home supposedly on vacation, and inform him that some gentleman has been arrested for drunken driving, what can he do about it, or some lady thinks she is entitled to a pension. She is only forty-eight years old but her children have all grown up and she is no longer getting the widow's pension. Just because she has been receiving it and the children are grown up she thinks she is still entitled to it, and the member must conceive some method of seeing that the pension is continued to her.
The duties of a member of parliament and the requests made of him should be considered by the people of Canada. The position of a member of the House of Commons should be set on a pedestal as high as any position occupied by any man in the country.
We talk about an increase of twenty per cent in judges' remuneration because of the service they render. I will say openly in the house today that the members of the House of Commons are badly underpaid. They are badly underpaid for the services rendered.. If any voter in any constituency thinks that he is going to get the kind of intelligence that he will need, not the kind that he wants, perhaps, but the kind that he needs for his benefit, he will have to pay more for that service.
There are men who have been talking and heckling in this house today who are very keenly pleased at the fact that there is another session in the offing in the fall and that they may replenish their depleted coffers. I am one of that group. I do not want to work for marbles, and I do not mind giving the best that I have in me in service to the people who sent me here, and I shall continue to do that, but I am going to be free to tell them that I am entitled to more pay. I am not going to beat around the bush about it as some men do.
What we need to do in this house is to show the people of the Dominion of Canada that in the position we occupy, or should occupy, we are representing all the people of Canada. By so doing we shall gain the respect for our position which is its due.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER MONDAY, JUNE 11
speechtext:
I have a few words to say on this motion. With all due respect to the hon. member who just took his seat, I think his remarks exemplify what a member of the House of Commons could do. The hon. member's voice and expression
Business of the House are such that if he went into competition with Jimmy Durante I think probably he could earn a lot of money. That is a compliment to the hon. member. I understand that he also had a splendid record in other realms, and I am proud to hear from the hon. member in connection with the duties of members of parliament.
In spite of the press statements, the duties of members of parliament have been carefully outlined by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and the work of the forthcoming fall session has been outlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I do submit, however, that there is a waste of time in this House of Commons. I have sat in a house for as long as nearly twenty years. There is a waste of time in debates in this house. There are some hon. members here who have been here a long time who do not indulge very much in debates, but when they do get up they do say something. There are other hon. members who have been here a long time because they have looked after the people of their constituencies. But the matter of serving a constituency is not jumping up in the house on every conceivable occasion.
If we are to amend the procedure in this House of Commons before the next session rolls around I should like to have statistics before us showing the time actually occupied by some of the professional orators. If they had not taken up so much time we would have been through with all the business by now. Because they have been here a long time, owing to their being lucky or through being skilful enough to spend all their time on politics, and thereby get re-elected, they think that they should make the job of a parliamentarian a profession. That is not our duty here. For instance, yesterday we had motions on second and third reading of a bill that were almost identical. It had to be voted on, twice. If the time taken in the house by certain members of the opposition were carefully calculated, and if we had it before us at the next session we might possibly consider changing some of the rules. Some of the suggestions of the hon. member for Eglinton could be very carefully considered by parliament and by the government.
The leader of the opposition objected to the statement being made that he was following the press. The leader of the opposition quoted from certain newspapers. I have read the two Ottawa papers and this paper from Montreal. There is no question in the world that they are nothing but Tory papers. I think they followed the leader of the opposition in their objection to the change that is proposed by the government. You cannot
3858	HOUSE OF
Business of the House pick up these papers and find properly quoted anything that a Liberal said. In my opinion they are nothing but Tory press and a Tory vehicle. I think they follow the leader of the opposition in their remarks criticizing the fact that members' indemnities are being raised.
With all due respect to the press-and I know some splendid fellows on the press- we do not find many members of the press elected to parliament. There are very few members of the House of Commons representing the press. In so far as the relative merits of the press and the parliament are concerned the people can judge. If there is any doubt as to the relative merits of the press and parliamentarians the ball game last night amply demonstrated who is superior.
In so far as the western members and the maritime members are concerned, the men who wrote these articles have not featured the actual position of those members. Not only have they left their homes, but they have to stay in Ottawa. Very few of them have been back to their homes during the whole of the session. For instance, two members from Saskatchewan have had to buy homes down here to get their young children at school and to keep them in their parents' care. Members from the maritimes and from Newfoundland are in the same position. They have to stay here. On the other hand, members from Ontario and Quebec can get home every week end-and some of them are very long week ends. They are also faced with something that possibly the press does not understand, and that is, that the closer you are to home the more difficulties you run into, and John Jones, his uncle and his aunt are on your doorstep, morning, noon and night, just as the previous speaker said.
Parliament is an institution. Following what the hon. member for Eglinton said I think we could shorten procedure in this House of Commons if certain members who have usurped the floor time after time, thinking that they are displaying ability and skill that are not possessed by other members, would refrain from jumping up on every conceivable occasion and taking up the time of the house in senseless debate.
I think that between sessions the cabinet might carefully consider overhauling some of the rules of the house. The session this fall will be an important one; important matters will have to be dealt with. Then, over and above the legislation to be introduced, we do not know what the war situation may be. Members would be subject to call if the war situation became worse.


Instead of being criticized in the house, I say the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the cabinet should be commended for having taken the stand they have taken. As has been said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), there are men working in factories, men working in mills in Hamilton and other places who, as unskilled labour, are earning more money than hon. members receive for their indemnity.
I disagree with what was said by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) with regard to lawyers. The law societies in all the provinces, and the judges, are not required to sit during what are known as the long vacations. The long vacation begins on July 1 and, except for summary trials before justices of the peace, there are no court sittings until September 15. And, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion that we sit here another two months listening to some of the speeches such as those we have been forced to listen to in the last four months nauseates some of the western members and, I believe, the maritimers, as well. That is a fallacious suggestion.
We have heard about the terrific heat of midsummer in Ottawa. We have not had that heat yet this summer; but as for accomplishing any real work in the House of Commons during July and August, particularly with respect to certain bills that have not yet been placed before the public, and which our constituents have not had an opportunity to study-and in this I include not only the matter of freight rates, but also the other bills the Prime Minister has mentioned-the prospect is not very bright. We want to discuss those measures with our constituents so that we may have their views and work refreshed in the fall.
In my opinion the government is to be complimented upon arranging matters as they have been arranged. For simple party reasons, the official opposition should have acquiesced, as have the other groups, in the suggested change for this year.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER MONDAY, JUNE 11
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last two speakers have made a real contribution to the debate. Anyone who will read their speeches carefully will see that they have pointed out many of the conditions facing members of parliament.
Morning sittings are distasteful to all hon. members; they are distasteful to members of the Social Credit group, because they constitute a heavy additional strain just when all conscientious members are pretty well worn down. But we know, as members of the Social Credit group, that in order to finish the business of the house we must

hold morning sittings; there is no use complaining about it. It is just part of what we have to take in our stride.
Governing Canada is an exceedingly complex and laborious task. This is true even in what might be called normal times; we are now in the most perilous of abnormal times. All this ought to be borne in mind when we are considering the problem of having a second session.
We are faced with problems of tremendous importance and of almost overwhelming intricacy.
As one example of the difficulty of governing Canada, look at our estimates. I do not wish to reflect upon anyone in the house, so far as his work here is concerned. In fact, I believe there is no one in the house upon whom reflection should be cast as regards using time. All one need do in this connection is consider the estimates. If the people of the country could see the big blue books of estimates members have on their desks, books completely filled with items, any one of most of which could occupy the time of the house for perhaps a week, and realize that members have to labour through those estimates during the course of a session, they would realize in part the problem facing us-and particularly the problem facing opposition groups who are expected to criticize adequately the estimates coming before the house.
There comes to my mind one item which hon. members will all have in their minds, I refer to the Department of Transport. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) came before the house with his estimates, prepared and ready to discuss them, and days and days were spent by opposition members on the discussion of only the first item. We did not make the slightest progress during those days, so far as getting the estimates through was concerned-and yet I believe every speech made was well worth making and was a contribution to the debate. If hon. members proceeded to examine each item as carefully as they examined the first one in the Department of Transport, we could not possibly hold enough sittings in a year to cover the estimates.
One question is this: What are we going to do about these estimates, most of which are as important as the first item in the Department of Transport?
I should like for a moment to turn to the press. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has quoted from certain newspapers throughout the country. In my opinion the writers of the editorials the leader of the opposition quoted simply went off the deep end. They indicated they did not
Business of the House know anything like what they ought to have known about the conduct of the affairs of the House of Commons; otherwise .they would not have made any such irresponsible statements as were read into the record this afternoon.
I think the time has come when someone ought to put our press to school, so that they would know something about the responsibility resting upon them. Anyone who reads almost any of the major newspapers of this country, on either side, finds himself reaching almost a state of disgust when he realizes the incompetency of the knowledge, understanding and thinking of the men who are writing these editorials.
Let me use one illustration: if members do not talk on the estimates, then according to certain newspapers they are weak, and are not doing their jobs; if they do talk, then they are wasting time and delaying the progress of the session! For some reason or other it seems there is scarcely a newspaper editorial writer in Canada who has been able to sense that fact, and to view the whole matter with equanimity and with a dispassionate soundness of thought. They do not seem to realize that everything they say has an effect upon the people, and has something to do with leaving the impression as to whether or not the House of Commons is a success.
As I said a moment ago, when we discuss the estimates we are accused of delaying progress; if we let them go through without criticism we are accused of being lax and negligent, so that we see headlines in certain papers condemning how the members have passed billions of dollars of estimates in one or two hours or one or two days! But all the members were trying to do was to get the estimates through so that the session could be finished in reasonable time. It is not that members do not want to discuss the estimates; under the circumstances they simply could not possibly take time to discuss them.
I suggest that every newspaper editor in the Dominion of Canada should obtain a copy of the estimates and then come forward with suggestions as to how the House of Commons can deal adequately with this volume of estimates in any length of session.
I am tempted to say something about the stand taken by the leader of the opposition, but I hesitate to do so. I did think, however, that after having been here as long as he has, and having been in public life as long as he has, he should have realized that a good many of the things he said would have been much better left unsaid. The position of
3860	HOUSE OF
Business of the House this group was well set forth by the leader of the Social Credit party on June 4 as recorded at pages 3668 and 3669 of Hansard. He agreed with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) completely with respect to holding a fall session. If he were here today- and he is unavoidably detained-I believe he would say that he would agree with the Prime Minister with respect to holding morning sittings. Therefore this group is completely behind the Prime Minister not only in holding a fall session but also in commencing morning sittings next week.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER MONDAY, JUNE 11
speechtext:
Just before the motion is put, there is a word I should like to say bearing directly on the question before us. I for one promise to be strictly in order and to talk about the motion now before the house, which calls for morning sittings starting at eleven o'clock next Monday morning. The reason I rise is that I want to put in a word for those whom the passing of this motion will directly affect.
[ refer to various groups of employees of the House of Commons. For a number of these groups it means additional work and additional hours. For one group in particular -and I refer to the Hansard staff-it not only means additional hours and additional work but it also means additional strain.
All of us have contacts with the members of the Hansard staff. I am sure all members will realize the truth of what I am saying, and will realize that in former sessions there have been times when we have been unfair to them because of the length of time during which morning sittings were held, and also because of the fact that toward the end of the session the tendency is to have a day or so when we sit right through meal hours. There are two suggestions I want to make. The first is that in view of this extra work I think consideration should be given to something in the nature of overtime pay. If there is no other way in which it can be done, at least it can be done by granting pay for a week or so after the session ends, and in view of the extra work I think members of the Hansard staff would be fully entitled to consideration of that nature.
The other suggestion I wish to make is that this time-and indeed in all future sessions-we should avoid, unless there is some dire emergency, going straight through on the last few days without rising for meal hours. I make that plea not on my behalf, not on behalf of the members, but on behalf of the Hansard staff who find those days really more of a strain that we should expect them to undergo.


What I have said about the Hansard staff applies to other groups, and I mention in particular the page boys. In view of the extra work we will be putting them to I think some special consideration should be given them. So far as they are concerned, I think we can leave it to His Honour, the Speaker, to find some way in which to make sure that they are compensated. I trust this will be done.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER MONDAY, JUNE 11
speechtext:
I am not going to speak very long. One hour and fifty-two minutes ago I bowed to the Speaker, and as a consequence of that bow he put a motion moved by me reading as follows:
That on and after Monday, June 11, 1951, until the end of the session, the house shall meet at eleven o'clock In the morning of each sitting day and that, in addition to the usual intermission at six o'clock p.m., there shall also be an intermission every day from one to three o'clock p.m.
In that hour and fifty-two minutes I have not heard anyone suggest that the motion should not be adopted. On the contrary, everybody has implied that it should be adopted. But notwithstanding that, there have been speeches that took an hour and fifty-two minutes on what the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) calls "kindred1 questions". Kindred questions are the explanation of the time that is taken in this house to transact the business that interests the country. The kindred questions were pretty carefully watched by the Speaker in this debate, and it is rather unusual that four or five times speakers were brought back to the matter that was before the house for discussion. It happens rather infrequently that in the discussion of these kindred questions the Speaker takes it upon himself to bring members back to the matter before the house.
I think that what has taken place here this afternoon is a very good explanation of why it becomes necessary at times to propose that there be three sittings a day in order to get through with the business that does have to be done. Those kindred questions are questions of considerable interest, but they are kindred. At the beginning of the session the standing of the parties was about 185 on this side and about seventy for all members of the opposition together. I have had a tabulation made of the time when kindred questions were under discussion in the budget debate and in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. On the budget 234 columns were taken by the 180 odd members of this party, and 331 were

taken by the seventy members of the other parties. On the speech from the throne 317 were taken by the Liberal members and 454 were taken by others. I am not complaining I am merely stating why it is that there comes a time when, to get the business of the house proceeded with, a motion of this kind has to be made. I submit it for the consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: I should like to direct to the Prime Minister a question of which I have given him notice. Is the Prime Minister prepared to arrange an interview for the delegation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REQUEST OF WESTERN FARMERS UNIONS FOR INTERVIEW WITH GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member sent notice to my office that he was going to ask this question, and therefore I was able to check the dates. The answer is as follows: On June 4 I received a telegram signed by Mr. J. L. Phelps containing a request that the government receive a delegation which would,
Inquiries of the Ministry according to the telegram, represent provincial farm union executives of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the British Columbia bloc accompanied by additional farmers, for the purpose of presenting a brief. I am not aware of what the brief contains, but the request stated that the delegation wished to present matters of urgent and immediate importance to western agriculture. I had a reply sent the next day, June 5, which stated that owing to the pressure of parliamentary duties it would not be possible to arrange an interview with the government but that the brief referred to in the request for the interview, when received, would be brought to the attention of those of my colleagues the organization might wish to have consider the representations.
I may add that members of the government met representatives of the farmers' unions of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta on April 9. Again on May 2 members of the government saw representatives of the farm organizations of western Canada. The delegation of May 2 included representatives of the federation of agriculture, the three pools, the united grain growers and the farmers' union. As nothing new to my knowledge has arisen since the May 2 meeting, I could see no urgent reason for arranging another interview at this time with organizations which form only a part of the federation of agriculture. When I receive this brief, if matters not already dealt with appear to be involved, the question of trying to find the time to receive a delegation can be reconsidered.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):

speechtext: The hon. member telephoned me this morning and said he proposed to ask this question. It has been reported to me that while agreement was not reached between the representatives of the fishermen and the merchants on minimum prices to be paid for the 1951 production of salted cod, there was no great difference between what the merchants were prepared to offer and what the fishermen considered to be the minimum they could accept. Agreement was reached to hold further meetings on a monthly basis throughout the season, and as the production and marketing picture clarifies it would seem likely that agreement on prices can be reached at a later date. I would point out that the chairman of the Newfoundland fisheries board, in calling this meeting, was simply providing a medium for the two groups to meet. The responsibility for decisions reached or not reached rests entirely with the fishermen and the trade.

When the committee rose last evening I had been discussing this item and I do not propose to take much more time, though this department is extremely important to my part of Canada. When it was organized it held out great promise to Nova Scotia and the maritimes generally, and I think our members are very sympathetic to the minister and are disposed to co-operate with him in every possible way. We are voting a large amount of money to this department, some $47,775,575, which includes vote No. 565 having to do with wartime housing, under which we are to vote $12,700,000. During the course of this discussion I would like the minister to state just what he is proposing that will be of assistance to my province and eastern Canada generally.
Last evening, in the few minutes at my disposal, I mentioned quite a number of items about which our people are concerned. I recognize that some of those matters are not covered by the estimates, but they have to do with the resources and development of Nova Scotia and I took it for granted that the minister would be concerned with them.
I was particularly discussing the dispersal of industry, which is of great interest to eastern Canada. Many representations have been made from all parts of the house with respect to expenditures made during the two great wars, and expressing the hope that due consideration or perhaps even special consideration would be given the outlying parts of Canada in the defence expenditures now being made. Not only was this view put forward by members in every part of this house; some senators expressed concern that more had not been done along this line. This does not come directly under the minister, I appreciate, but after all he is the minister directly responsible for the interests of Nova Scotia, and I look to him to take an interest in this. What has been

done up to the present has been very disappointing, but we are still hopeful that special appropriations will be assigned to eastern Canada. I noticed an announcement a few days ago that the enormous sum of $50 million was to be spent in constructing a chemical plant in Alberta. A few days ago I asked the Minister of Defence Production what was being done in Nova Scotia in regard to chemicals development, and he gave the encouraging reply that it was being considered but he could not yet make an announcement. I hope the Minister of Resources and Development will be able to make some announcement in this respect.
There are many other matters which are concerning the people of eastern Canada but I do not know that there is any necessity for me to refer to them on this occasion as no doubt other hon. members will do so. Other items of expenditure will be discussed in detail as they are called and I do not know that I need say anything more on this first administration item.
The Department of Resources and Development holds out great promise, or it did when it was organized, to the people of my constituency, to the people of Nova Scotia and to the people of eastern Canada. I look forward to hearing a specific statement by the minister as to just what he proposes to do under these estimates to assist this part of Canada.
There is still a considerable amount of unemployment and many of our people are being attracted away from home to central Canada. We feel strongly that this should not take place. It is the primary duty of the minister to see that employment is given to these people where their homes are and that they be not attracted away with their families following in due course. It is the primary duty of this department and of the government in general to see that there is a fair distribution of industry at a time when there is so much production in Canada. This should be done as quickly as possible.
It has been stated in the house that members from the maritime provinces are continually complaining. I do not think that that is a fair interpretation of the appeals we made during the last war and since, and are making at the present time. I think it is recognized by many who do not live in the maritime provinces that those provinces have not received proper consideration from this government and from some previous governments. We have the resources and the manpower and we certainly have contributed our part to the formation of Canada.
There would have been no Dominion of Canada had it not been for a statesman who
Supply-Resources and Development came from the maritime provinces. There would have been no Dominion of Canada had we not formed part of it. Many people in Nova Scotia have been disappointed with the results, but I assure members of the house that we are still good Canadians and are going to play our part within the bounds of Canada. We make this special plea to the minister whose estimates are now before the committee, to the government in general and to the membership of the house, that more attention be given to the needs of our people in eastern Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have one
or two comments I should like to make but I can assure you that they will not be long. They have to do chiefly with conservation. I believe the minister, and no doubt all hon. members, will agree that possibly conservation is the most important thing in Canada today. When we speak of conservation we think immediately of our forests and what has happened to them. Someone told me recently that as a result of carelessness last year enough timber was burned in Canada to build a city the size of Montreal. If that is so then very definite measures should be taken to ensure the future wealth of our forests.
I understand that when the white man came to this country there were nine inches of top soil. As a result of the destruction of our forests by fire and improper cutting that top soil is now less than six inches deep. That is a very serious matter. If our forests are not properly conserved our top soil will gradually disappear. Top soil is the most important soil in the country.
With all this I couple the question of the conservation of game fish. I am sure that the minister's department has this matter seriously in mind. I do not think I can approach this subject more strongly than the department is probably approaching it at the present time, but I do feel that those who hunt and fish should have instilled in them, and we should keep on instilling in them, the fact that they should not shoot any more than they intend to eat. They should not shoot simply for the pleasure of shooting. This applies to all types of game and wildlife. It applies particularly to game fish, and here I am not dealing with the fish that would come under the Minister of Fisheries. He has strong ideas on conservation and he has been showing a great interest in this matter during the past twelve months.
If it has not already been done, a special effort should be made by the department along these lines. Education should be carried on through the schools in order to reach
3864	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Resources and Development our younger sportsmen, and there should be some form of continuous public campaign. Not only do we need our wildlife, we also need the money that is obtained as a result of that blessing. I venture to say that a large part of the United States money that we obtain is obtained from those who are interested in hunting and fishing. If we are to preserve that heritage very definite steps will have to be taken to see that these resources are not depleted.
We have seen what has happened in other countries. We have seen various species of wildlife disappear. We have in this country streams which at one time carried great numbers of salmon but which today carry none. As I said, I am not going to speak strongly or at length on this matter. I am sure the minister's mind is clear on the subject, and I believe that he feels the same as I do. When you discuss the conservation of resources you are discussing a matter that touches everybody. After all, the resources of each province in this dominion are extremely vital. When we see any natural resources being made away with by any means, we get a little bit worried. I am sure the minister has not had the opportunity of studying the bill that is going to be put before the legislature in St. John's, Newfoundland; but it deals with a great many of these resources over which the minister here has control. I hope the minister will be in a position to tell me what stumpage on wood is being paid in each province of Canada this year. I should like those figures if I could get them. I have a special reason for wanting them. An attempt is being made to give to a corporation a large area of the province of Newfoundland at a stumpage rate of fifty cents. To me that seems to be an extraordinarily low price. It is a matter that comes within the minister's purview, I should think. I should like him to let me have a comment on this matter and, if he can, to let me have the stumpage that is paid ' in the other provinces that are cutting wood.

I have a small but specific
matter that I should like to bring to the minister's attention. It has to do with a national park, namely the national park at Waskesiu in northern Saskatchewan. Three or four years ago I had occasion to make some complaint on behalf of the people whom I represent in the city of Saskatoon and who, I may say, use this park as a summer vacation ground; and a fine vacation ground it is. At that time a great many

people were using what are commonly called shack tents-a movable affair and semipermanent, if I may call it that-'which they took down and stored away in the fall of the year and put back again when they went back for the next summer. May I say that those people believed that they were receiving rather scant treatment on the part of the park authorities. They felt that they were being edged back from the lots which they occupied temporarily and that these grounds which they had previously occupied were being given to people who were willing to build cottages of a more permanent type.
I want to pay tribute to the superintendent of that particular park. Since Mr. Strong has been there, we have found a decided improvement. The people for whom I was concerned previously have had little reason for complaint; and so far as I know they have not made any.
There was, however, one incident which happened this year and which was brought to the minister's attention, and as to which, in correspondence with me, he did not answer. Whether that was an oversight on the part of his officials, I do not know; but I am going to bring it to his attention again. To these people who had these temporary quarters an opportunity was given to get lots upon which they might build a little bit more permanent type of thing. There was a big demand for those lots, and the matter was decided by drawing certain numbers out of a hat. My correspondent tells me that there were only 70 of these lots available whereas there were over 100 applications for them. That is reasonable enough.
The point that I want to make is that these people, in whose interests I speak, have had these grounds for a number of years. This man in particular had the ground since the year 1928. When it came to settling as to who would get these sites upon which to build this particular type of cabin, the names were put in a hat. But the names were put in a hat by the general public as well as by the people who had previously occupied the grounds. His contention-and it is a contention which was totally overlooked, may I say, in the answer of the minister-was that these people who had occupied these grounds for a period of years-and my constituent had done so since 1928-had a priority over the general public. That was his opinion, and it is my opinion.
When this matter was brought to the minister's attention, he replied that he sympathized with my friend who had not been lucky in the draw of the numbers out of the hat and that my friend would have the opportunity again, when the numbers

were again put in the hat perhaps a year from now, to get ownership of some other lot in some other grounds somewhere else. That is not the point. That is evading the issue. The point is this. Should these people who have had those lots for years and years not have some priority over the general public? That is the question that I should like to bring to the minister's attention, and I should like him to tell me what he thinks about that particular situation.

In Prince Albert national park at Waskesiu, there was a need for further campsites mentioned by the hon. member, and a new area was opened up. The determination of who would have the privilege of occupying sites in the new area was made by draw, which seemed to be the fairest arrangement.
Mr. Chairman, might I interrupt the minister long enough to say that I do not agree with him when he says that it was the fairest arrangement.
That is a matter of opinion.

Does the minister think those lots should have been open to the public when people who had been there for ten, twelve or fourteen years had to submit to the chance of a draw as to whether or not they could get one of these lots?

If the hon. member had
allowed me to continue, as he did not choose to do, I would have said that the people who have been there for the period of time be mentioned still have the right to remain where they are now and that these new areas are available to new people coming in or to anybody who wishes to take a chance on the draw to change from where he is now to one of the sites in the new area.

I just want to say a few words on this item and to ask the minister a question. We were greatly interested last year in the opening of Fundy park in New Brunswick. I think we were the last province in Canada to have a park. Newfoundland was not part of Canada at the time that the parks were considered previously. We were indeed pleased that our park was opened in New Brunswick. I remember that in 1937 or 1938, I think it was, the parks were opened in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. At that time and previously I had pressed in the house for the opening of a park in New Brunswick. I felt that it was unfortunate that so many years had passed before it took place, and that we lost a great opportunity of tourist trade over those years. There was, however, difficulty over a site between the federal government and the
