Supply-Resources and Development province, mostly, I think, owing to the fact that the province could not decide on a site.
I may tell the minister that there were some complaints. I should like to have the minister's attention if I may, while I am speaking. There was some complaint over the ceremony at Fundy park last year. I may say that I am not blaming the minister personally at all, because I know that, when he goes into a province to open a park or any other public institution, arrangements are usually made by those in the province. But he must have been struck himself, I think, by the fact that the opening of Fundy park was entirely a political matter. There was not one-
Not political.
It was entirely political.
No, not political.

There was not one Conservative who took any part in the function. The leader of the opposition in the province of New Brunswick was not even extended the courtesy of being asked to sit on the platform although there were twenty other members and officials and mayors of different cities and towns who were asked. Mr. Mackay, after he came to the park at the very last minute on that day, was asked if he would come up and sit on the platform; but the courtesy had not been extended to him previously.
I dislike interjecting a personal matter, but the Fundy park is a part of my constituency, just as it is a part of the constituency of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, and I was not extended the courtesy of having an invitation.

If the hon. member will permit me to say a word to avoid a long debate, I should like to extend to him and to the colleagues of his party an apology. At the time of the arrangement I did not know that there had been that oversight but I learned of it since, and I was just as disappointed as he was. I am very sorry it happened. With regard to the remark about its being political, it was not intended to be political. I believe anyone who was there that day would support me in saying that there was no political complexion to any of the proceedings. I say again, I am very sorry that the members of the opposition concerned were not invited, and we shall certainly see to it that such a thing does not happen again.

The minister just bears out exactly what I said at the outset. I was satisfied that the minister had no intention
386S

Supply-Resources and Development that any discourtesy should be given to anyone. We look on our public park as something that belongs to all the people. There was considerable criticism in New Brunswick, and there is today, over the fact that this courtesy was not extended to members of opposition parties.
The minister says it was not political. Well, I listened to the speeches. I know that the chairman glorified the premier of the province and the premier glorified-
The leader of the opposition would have done that.
-the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The Minister of Veterans Affairs came on and glorified the present Minister of Resources and Development.
I do not remember that.

And so on right down the line. It was just a glorification of everyone. I was pleased to hear my good friend the hon. member for Saint John-Albert glorified, a man who had absolutely nothing to do with the park. He was not here in the house when the matter was brought up.
I have been here ever since the work started.

I do not intend to elaborate this matter any further. I am satisfied that if the minister has anything more to do with matters of this kind in the province of New Brunswick he will see that courtesy and justice are extended to everyone. I have that confidence in him.
There is one thing that I should like to say about the park. We are indeed pleased to have it. It is a wonderful tourist attraction, but there is a complaint that there is no way of getting to it without great inconvenience. The money that has been spent has been justified except for the fact that the people cannot get there without travelling through clouds of dust. I know that a great many United States tourists who come into the province of New Brunswick start off for our Fundy national park. They have to breathe and eat dust for about fifteen or twenty miles. They come back disappointed and disgusted. It is certainly a great drawback. When looking into this matter I hope that the minister will provide a proper road through the park. I do not know whether it is his responsibility or the responsibility of the provincial government.
Provincial.

I understand that it is provincial. After establishing such a splendid park in New Brunswick I hope that the minister will use his influence to try and see that the

provincial government does something toward getting people there in comfort, and, as I say, without having to eat dust for fifteen or twenty miles.

I notice that $10,000 was provided under this item last year for the province of Newfoundland, but no amount is provided this year. I believe that nothing has been done. Was the $10,000 spent that was provided last year? If so, what was it spent for? Why is nothing provided this year? Is it the intention to establish a park? If so- and I presume it is-has anything been done about deciding on the area? If so, what has been done? The minister has had this matter raised on several occasions. I feel it is about time that we had a pretty clear-cut answer on the matter.

Under that vote last year certain investigations of possible sites were carried out, but no park has been established. We have had no formal offer of an area from the government of Newfoundland, which is part of the arrangement under which any park is established, and no final steps have been taken toward the establishment of a national park in Newfoundland.
Is the provincial government no-t anxious to establish a national park?
I of course cannot say whether the Newfoundland government is anxious to establish a park. They asked us to investigate certain areas, and officials of the department have done that.
And the investigation is completed?
That phase of the investigation is completed, at any rate. A report has been prepared, and it is available in the department. I have not studied it yet myself.

How long has that been completed?
Mr Winters: Since the first of this year.
And no action has been taken?
That is right.

I was interested to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Royal with respect to Fundy national park and also with respect to the road, because some of the roads going through the county which forms part of my hon. friend's constituency are rather dusty. I realize at the same time that this is not a responsibility of the Minister of Resources and Development, although we in New Brunswick would like him to arume at least part of the responsibility. His department could very easily see that in the

interests of promoting this most splendid park which is located in my constituency-
Not altogether.

-a gesture could be made by offering to pay at least half of the cost of the road leading into the park from my hon. friend's constituency.
I was also interested to hear my hon. friend's comment on the opening ceremonies.
I was present at these ceremonies. I enjoyed them very much, and I am sure that he did as well. Perhaps we did not have the leader of the opposition on the platform-I thought he had been there. I am sure he did receive an invitation to attend the opening ceremonies.
Yes, but not to take part.
Did my hon. friend not receive an invitation to attend the opening ceremonies?

Since my hon. friend has asked me, yes, I did. What I was complaining about was that in the ceremonies themselves no invitation was extend d to the leader of the opposition or to anyone else except Liberals. In over twenty on the platform there was one Conservative who happened to be the mayor of Moncton, and it was generally understood that it was a very discourteous matter right through the piece.

It is all very well for the hon. member for Royal to say that he was not on the program. Neither was there any member of parliament nor any member of the legislature nor any member from the Conservative party. On the platform that day was the Minister of Resources and Development. He could hardly have been denied a place there. Then there was the Minister of Labour. He could hardly have been denied a place. The premier of the province could hardly have been denied a place.
None of them should have been.

And members of the legislature from the county of Albert, who worked so hard to have the park there, as a matter of courtesy were asked to be on the platform. And I am very proud that the courtesy was extended to me, because the park was in my constituency.
I rise to a point of order. I am sure the hon. member wishes to be correct. The park is also partly in my constituency; I do not know whether he knows that or not.

Mr. Chairman, if the park is partly in the hon. member's constituency,
Supply-Resources and Development then I regret very much that I have not yet been able to visit that tiny corner of the park.
That is hardly fair.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You are making it worse.

No, I am not making it worse, at all. The hon. member for Charlotte was not on the platform, nor was the hon. member for Northumberland. The hon. member for Royal says that we must institute economies and save money; yet if the platform were built-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: How much did it cost to put you on the platform?

If the platform were built big enough to take in all the political parties, every member of every political party in New Brunswick, I am sure the hon. member for Royal would have some word of criticism.
What I would point out to the minister in regard to Fundy national park has something to do with the rate of wages being paid to the' employees of the park. I notice that from time to time people are engaged in what are known as casual labour positions, which do not come under civil service commission regulations. I have had complaints from some of those people and from other interested parties in different parts of the province who, after visiting the park, have pointed out that there are workmen there in responsible positions, or positions which would scarcely be classified as labour, and who come within the wage rate which is known as the prevailing rate in any locality. They are working perhaps ten hours a day and getting sixty-five cents an hour.
Would the minister look into this and ascertain if there are not people working at Fundy national park at wages which hardly compensate them for the amount of responsibility they must take and the long hours they work to retain their positions. I know of one instance where an expert garage mechanic was employed to look after machinery. A good deal of expensive machinery is used in connection with the park, and maintenance work generally. After warning the department on several occasions, this man was forced to seek employment elsewhere, because of the low rate of wages. I hope this item will come to the minister's attention before the park is used to any extent this summer. I am sure the people in that locality would appreciate the minister's attention in the matter, as indeed I would.
Another matter which has been brought to my attention on various occasions may not come exclusively within the jurisdiction of the minister. However, it has to do with the post office in the town of Alma.

Supply-Resources and Development
That is not in this vote.

speechtext: If it is not within the scope of this vote, the hon. member cannot discuss it.

I shall save it for another
occasion.
Is it correct to say that the minister is prepared to establish a national park in Newfoundland as soon as the provincial government makes the land available?

I am not prepared to say at this moment that that is correct. The matter of establishing a national park is something that must be done by mutual agreement of the federal and provincial governments, the two major parties concerned. The purpose would be to set aside an area in a province for the use of all Canadians, so that they may enjoy themselves, and so that a certain area may be retained in its natural state in perpetuity.
We have had some discussion with the government of Newfoundland as to the desirability of a national park there. However it has not been finally determined whether an expenditure of money could best be made in establishing a national park in that province at this time. That does not mean to say that it is not the best way of spending the money, nor do I say that it is the best way. It is a matter we have to consider, and we must decide whether at this particular time there might be some other way or ways in which an equivalent amount of money might be spent to better advantage for the benefit of the citizens of Newfoundland and of Canada as a whole. The matter has not yet been finally decided.
Is it because the provincial government was not prepared to spend the money on this project, and felt it could spend the money to better advantage in another direction, that nothing has been done?
I am not prepared to say in this house what is in the minds of members of the government of Newfoundland.
To your knowledge.
I am simply saying that it is a matter of policy for the province of Newfoundland which has not yet been determined.

Mr. Chairman, in the few moments remaining before six o'clock I should like to express a word of appreciation to the minister and the government for the decision taken recently to take over Citadel hill in Halifax as a national historic site. I believe the procedure of taking the responsibility for this property from the Department of National Defence and placing it under the

historic sites and monuments board is a proper one, and one which has been welcomed not only in Halifax but throughout Nova Scotia.
Citadel hill, and Fort George, which is the fortification crowning Citadel hill, constitute in truth a most historic site. It is the central part of the old fortification dating back to the founding of the city of Halifax in 1749. The restoration and maintenance of the fortifications and work on Citadel hill will, I am sure, be of great interest and benefit to the whole of Canada. Not only is it an historical location, but it is also an extremely beautiful one, commanding a view of the city, the magnificent harbour and far out to sea.
Therefore I wish to express this word of congratulation and appreciation to the minister and to the government on behalf of the people of Halifax, who have had this matter at heart for many years. If anyone had any doubt as to the wisdom and farsightedness of the decision taken by the government in this connection, I am sure those doubts have been more than resolved by the findings of the royal commission which has dealt with this matter.

Mr. Chairman, before you call it six o'clock, out of deference to the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, and so that the reply to his question may be found near the question, for anyone consulting Hansard, I would say that the rates for the people he had in mind in the national park are established after consultation with the Department of Labour, and have regard to the prevailing rates in the area. The rates for the park are under revision now, and it is likely they will be revised before they are implemented this year.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Henderson (Kingston City) moved
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 354, to incorporate First Canadian Reinsurance Company.
Mr. Speaker, might I ask the sponsor for an explanation of this bill?

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to incorporate this company to carry on the business of insurance and reinsurance as is outlined in the title and in the bill. I might say that reinsurance is a common practice in the insurance business. I am told that the present intention of the principals is that their business will be along the line of reinsurance to begin with, and they will do business in all types of insurance save and except life insurance. The bill is drafted in the usual form and complies with the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. I understand it has the approval of the superintendent of insurance and I recommend that it be accorded second reading and referred to the banking and commerce committee.
Would the sponsor mind stating what the subscribed capital is and the capital set-up of the company?

I believe the capital set-up is contained in section 7 of the bill. There can be no meeting of the directors until $100,000 has been subscribed in bona fide subscriptions, and no business will be commenced until $250,000 has been subscribed in a bona fide manner.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

Canadian Pacific Railway Company
the second reading of Bill No. 356, respecting Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Could we have an explanation of this bill?

The purpose of this bill is to
enable the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to carry out the terms of an agreement with the Alberta Coal Company providing for the purchase of fourteen miles of railroad recently constructed. As hon. members know, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is incorporated by an act of this parliament and therefore comes under the dominion Railway Act, which requires that before a railway company may purchase or lease the railway of another company it must have the approval of parliament. The object of this bill is to grant the company this power.
Would the hon. member permit a question before he takes his seat?

Yes, when I am through. The line the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will acquire if authorized by parliament is a spur line recently constructed by the Alberta Coal Company connecting with the Canadian Pacific main line near Halkirk, which is somewhere between Calgary and Edmonton in Alberta. This spur line was constructed to enable the coal company to get its coal out by rail. The agreement which has been entered into by the coal company and the railway company is very much in the interests of the coal company. That company is not in the railway business and does not want to take over the responsibility of operating and maintaining this line. It will also enable the people in that area to open up a more or less new industry. As I have said, the coal company prefers to have this spur owned and operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway, with which it connects.
I therefore suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this bill be given second reading and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where the circumstances surrounding the agreement and other relevant matters may be gone into.
Do I understand the coal company built the line and owns all the shares in it?

I am not sure who owns the shares of this line, though I understand the line is owned by the coal company. However, before the committee witnesses will be ready to give the answers to all these questions, and I believe that information can be obtained much more readily when the matter is before the committee.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 5, 1951, consideration of the motion of Mr. Robinson for the second reading of Bill No. 118, to incorporate Border Pipeline Corporation, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Herridge.

Mr. Speaker, from time to time in this house we have had debates with respect to oil and gas pipe lines. It may be thought strange that a maritimer should have something to say on this bill to incorporate this company, which is seeking permission to build and operate a pipe line. My reason for taking part in the debate is to express the opinion I have formed after listening to those who have spoken in opposition to this bill. One must consider the remarks that have been made. With one exception all those who have spoken on this bill have opposed it because they do not consider it in the interests of Canada first. The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has impressed me from time to time with his arguments on these bills, in which he has indicated that he is looking out for Canada first.
I am taking the stand that I oppose this bill on similar grounds. I have nothing against the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill. I know him as a good member of this house, and I had hoped that he would go back to his incorporators and have them change this bill by making the route allCanadian, instead of having it take oil or gas to the United States. I try to look after the interests of Canada first, and with that in mind I believe we should ask ourselves what we are legislating for. In the closing days of a session, and indeed at other times as well, bills are brought hurriedly before committees of the house and adopted. Later, as has happened in other years, we find that certain bills should not have been adopted, because they were found not to be altogether in the interests of Canada first.
Many reasons could be given for taking that stand. I am going to give a few, which I hope may keep hon. members from voting for this bill. It is a great pleasure to be in this house and hear various hon. members from different provinces boosting-I could say boasting, but I think boosting is a better word-about the natural resources of their own districts and of Canada as a whole. The natural resources of Canada are something that any hon. member can be proud to boast about. These resources are barely scratched. The natural resources of Canada are great

indeed. Our production of agricultural products is one of the greatest in the world. Look at our forests. We can see at a glance that they constitute another great natural resource. Then we have minerals of all kinds. We have the finest fish that can be caught in waters anywhere in the world.
These are things that are worthy of consideration. In referring to our mineral wealth I am reminded of the gold rush to the Yukon in 1898, the greatest gold rush in the history of America. There have been other gold rushes, but the 1898 gold rush to the Yukon was the greatest that Canada or the United States had ever seen. The reason why so many made such great efforts to get to the Yukon was the hope that gold could be practically picked up from the stream. But they were all sure of one thing, that no expensive mining operations would be required.
Then came the discovery of oil in western Canada, particularly in Alberta and the oil rush is on today to that part of Canada. There is a rush also by different corporations to obtain, as it were, a complete monopoly in connection with the sale or export of this oil. In passing legislation of this type our first thought should be to see that the province that produces the oil is served first. Our second thought should be to see that the provinces adjoining are given an opportunity to use the oil to develop their manufacturing and other industries within the province. Then if there is a surplus it can be piped elsewhere to those other parts of Canada which require oil for the production of power and for manufacturing purposes. They should have the third right to the use of this great natural resource.
Why does this bill not contain a provision that the pipe line shall be routed through Canadian territory to British Columbia and the Pacific coast, to pass through Vancouver and other places? If that had been provided I think this bill would receive the support of the house because it would then be serving Canada first. If the pipe line were built in that way it would supply the Pacific coast. If there was a surplus it could easily be extended to the United States to serve our good neighbours to the south.
However, we find that this pipe line bill does not appear to be in the best interests of Canada. When speaking on the pipe lines some hon. members have referred to the Canadian Pacific railway. The Canadian Pacific railway served Canada first. When it was proposed to build that railroad from the Atlantic to the Pacific there was considerable difference of opinion among some of the most outstanding British, United States and
Border Pipeline Corporation Canadian engineers, some of them contending that it was impossible to build this railroad over an all-British route to the Pacific coast.
There must have been some men in British Columbia who have the same idea as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). At that time British Columbia had not entered into union with the rest of Canada and the people there stated that unless they received a guarantee from the railroad company that the railway would be built on all-British territory to the Pacific coast, they would not enter union.
Is it?
This was carried into effect and that is the reason why today the Canadian Pacific serves Canada first and links up British Columbia as one of the provinces of the dominion.
What about Maine?

Another route could have been chosen but how much better off are the people of Canada that some men insisted that this railroad should be built on all-British territory or, as we call it today, on allCanadian soil from coast to coast. I have not sufficient information at my command to go into the further details of this bill, but I think our main reason for stopping its passage is that it does not serve Canada first. If it is to serve Canada first it must be built to the Pacific on Canadian soil. As I said a moment ago, if British Columbia does not require all the oil and there is a surplus it can be piped down to our neighbours to the south.
Another matter that I wish to make just a few remarks on is this. For many years we have been great sellers of foodstuffs and exporters of our raw materials. Here we have a raw material that we must not lose out on by exporting. The war brought to Canada an awakening; even if she had to suffer in two disastrous wars, at the same time Canada awoke and found herself ready to manufacture-something that was not done, except on a very small scale, prior to 1914. Canada can now be looked upon as one of the great, young manufacturing nations owing to the fact that we were forced into it. We have raw materials of every kind suitable for manufacturing. Why not manufacture that raw material into products that we need in this country instead of exporting the raw material and then bringing it back in its made-up condition, with our people having to pay five times the price they would have had to pay if they had adopted the principle of manufacturing their own raw materials into the products that they require?

Border Pipeline Corporation
Foodstuffs are a little bit different. We can supply our own people. But, on the other band, the greater the manufacturing industries grow, the greater would be our home market for our own production of foodstuffs. In closing my remarks, I just wish to add this. We all believe that Canada is a great young nation, Canada today is progressing probably more rapidly than any other country in the world. While Canada may be small in population, in area it is the third largest country in the world. As I have already said, it has the greatest resources of any country in the world. Why not let us see that these resources are used for Canadians and for Canada first? Consider what it would do for men of labour. If this pipe line were going to be built in Canadian territory through to the Pacific, the men of labour would have the opportunity of building it. They would also have a further opportunity of seeing that it was kept in repair. Then last but not least, when that raw material would get to British Columbia, there could be large refineries that would employ a great number of men. Surely we in this house should look to the interests of the labourer, to give him more work, and to produce more comfort for him. The only way by which we can do that is by having pipe lines and similar things serve Canada first before they serve other nations.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that others will follow me and speak against the passing of this bill, so that we will be assured that the interests of the labourers of Canada, as well as the best interests of all Canadians, will be properly served by having an all-Canadian pipe line route to the Pacific coast.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is to create a company known as the Border Pipeline Corporation. I believe that this company is actually sponsored by a group of people south of the border who have had a tremendous amount of experience in the construction and operation of pipe line companies. Undoubtedly they have gone to a firm of solicitors in this country and have had them prepare a charter to be presented to the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada. I believe that the solicitors must have instructed these gentlemen south of the border with regard to the powers of the members of the House of Commons and with regard to their duties towards the people of Canada, and have told them that it was not a one-way street, that it was not simply a duty that we owed to our guests and to the people desirous of coming to our country to utilize our tremendous natural resources. We must think not only

of courtesy to people coming to our country from the other side, but we must also think of the security and the welfare of the people of the Dominion of Canada.
Bearing that fact in mind, the situation reminds me somewhat of that which would confront you if you invited people to come to your home for dinner, and when they arrived you found that they did not like the dinner you were serving and started to dictate the kind and class of food they would prefer rather than the type you were serving. Much as we desire development of our great resources by our friends to the south and much as we need their aid and experience, we still do not want them to criticize too severely the food that we are offering. As a matter of fact, in this case it almost seems that they do not want to eat at all unless it is something they can provide for themselves. They must learn that we are the host. We have the natural resources. It is our food, it is our table, and it is our home that they are entering. They must therefore be content with some of the food we are offering and with the terms on which we are offering it.
The duty of the members of the House of Commons is, wherever possible, to see that the resources of this country produce as much profit and welfare for the people of Canada as they do for the users in foreign lands. We want to use our natural resources for the development of our factories and the development of our labour markets. We certainly cannot do that if we hurry our resources by the shortest possible route from the source of supply to the foreign country to which we are shipping our natural resources.
It has been gone into fairly thoroughly that by transporting the natural resources such as oil to the users in not too extravagant a manner, over a sane and reasonable distance, we are creating employment for the people of the Dominion of Canada. That does not seem to be asking too much when you realize the offering we have to make. It is worth millions. It will make millions. Oil has made millions for operators such as the applicants for this pipe line charter, in various parts of the world. One oil-producing country almost produced the spark that set off the third world war. That gives an idea of the importance of this natural resource we have. We find the President of the United States walking very gingerly and talking in whispers in order not to offend an oil-producing country that is not quite as far advanced in its general operation of industry as is the Dominion of Canada. Yet the applicants at this time would almost have you believe that we are wrong in demanding that they at least transport this oil by an

all-Canadian route and agree to operate, with regard to running their pipe line, on identically the same basis as other applicants for charters are willing to operate. I cannot see that we are asking them to do something that is unusual or anything that might materially change their profits. I do not think there is any reason why they could not operate at a profit or that there is any reason that they might lose the money they have already invested in investigating the potentialities of this pipe line. We are not asking anything unreasonable on behalf of the people of Canada. We are asking for an assurance from the applicants for this charter that if it is granted they will havb written into it the proviso that the pipe line or lines for the transmission or transportation of oil or natural gas, or artificial gas or liquid, or gaseous products or by-products thereof, shall be built entirely within Canada.
I do not know and I have not heard of any persons giving any logical reason why that should not be inserted in the agreement if this charter is granted. Too frequently in the past we have given away our great natural resources without due consideration of Canada. We have given those resources to foreign users. We have watched our population grow very slowly when it should have gone ahead at a rate at least twice as fast as it has progressed in the past fifty years. There have been times when we have wondered what we could employ our people at, and how we could utilize our terrific natural resources. Amongst the people in power there seemed to be an epidemic at times. Their desire was to get rid of those resources without due consideration <to the coming generations of Canadians who would need them and who would be able and willing to develop them. We know that our forests have been denuded of the natural wealth which was given to us.
We now find ourselves in the position where the greatest nation in the world is willing to buy Canadian produced newsprint, not simply pulpwood, at a very handsome figure. The purchase of this newsprint goes a great distance towards balancing our economic condition with other great nations. We do know that it was not very long ago that our pulpwood was being shipped across the border to the south in tremendous quantities at very little income to Canada or Canadians. Through the foresight and determination of men in power in Canada a few years ago the tables have been entirely turned. Canada is still a producer of pulpwood. Canadians have built paper mills. Canadians by thousands are now employed in turning out the finished product, paper, and are shipping that product finished and corn-80709-2464
Border Pipeline Corporation plete ready for use to the vast paper presses of the United States at a very handsome figure, which means considerable and well deserved profits to the Canadian people.
If we did not have this tremendous paper wealth, which is almost exclusive to the Canadian people, just how much purchasing power would the Canadian dollar have in regard to commodities which we are forced to purchase in the United States? I believe I am safe in saying that we would be paying almost four, five or ten times as much on exchange as we are paying at the present time if it had not been for the perseverance and foresight of men in public life on matters pertaining to the vast wealth in the forests of Canada. We are not asking any more than these men asked in the past. We are simply asking that someone pay a reasonable amount, and that Canadians obtain as much of the profit as is reasonable from the discovery of oil in Alberta. The people who are desirous of obtaining this wealth should pay this amount.
It is unfortunate that the solicitors for this corporation, knowing the attitude of the members of the House of Commons-because they have expressed their opinions previously in the debates-did not tap their clients on the shoulder and say: "Let us hurry the assurance down to Ottawa that we do intend to run an all-Canadian pipe line, because the gentlemen in Ottawa apparently are determined. They are not going to bend their knee to your whim just because you would like it that way." This debate could have been avoided, and the great expense to the Canadian taxpayers could have been avoided, if that had been done. I do hope that the members of the House of Commons will have the fortitude to stand up and continue to block this charter until such time as the people who desire to use our wealth are willing to accede to our terms, which I do not believe to be unreasonable.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate chiefly because I feel compelled to do so.
Oh, oh.

The compulsion though, Mr. Speaker, is not, as some hon. members may suggest by their raucous laughter, from anything else but the conscience that I feel every hon. member has, because all we must do is look around at hon. members here this evening and see the obvious interest that is displayed in this matter. When one does that he realizes how their conscience must be pricking them steadily as we discuss this most important bill.

Border Pipeline Corporation
I am quite certain, that all hon. members, when they attend here on evenings like this and see such an important measure being discussed, must ask themselves: What are we here for? Especially is that so after the discussion that went on this afternoon at such great length on the duties of the members of the House of Commons and the stipends they receive for the very arduous duties that they perform. Then I say to myself again this evening when an important measure like this is being considered: How very obvious the interest is among the hon. members who are listening to me now.
I now intend to deal with various phases of the matter. I expect that any matter that has been left over from former discussions will be considered somewhat repetitious, but I am sure that a good thing cannot be repeated too often. For that reason, if I do repeat myself, and certainly if I repeat some of the expressions of my colleague, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure), who displayed this evening a world of wisdom in the excellent address he gave on this matter, I hope that I will be pardoned, because it is not often that I have the pleasure of hearing the hon. member for Queens talking at length as he talked this evening. We do not often get that pleasure. Having heard him this evening I do say that we should have it many, many more times, because he has contributed to the discussion and to the wisdom of hon. members this evening something that we did not have before, and something that certainly the newer members of the house did not have before. It is only when you have the wisdom of the ages given by the sages of the house that the younger members can possibly hope to embody what this thing means in all its moods.
Carried.
Can you not bear with me a little longer? This bill to incorporate Border Pipeline Corporation was, passed by the Senate in March.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I remind the hon. member that we are discussing the amendment.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Well, I just wish to look at the actual title of the bill. I understand of course that we are discussing the amendment. But that amendment gets right down to the principle I should like to discuss in the house this evening, namely the principle of the conservation of natural resources. This is a matter we must consider fully, because, after all, it must be kept in mind that trees are a crop; they are cut down and grow back again. Wheat and other cereals grown by the farmers are crops that can be cut down. But there are resources 

such as oil and minerals that are taken out of the earth and are not put back. That is the end of them. Either they are used properly or they are lost forever.
If we are to use our natural resources we must be convinced in our own mind that we are using them for the benefit of the people -all the people, and not only a small section of them. The amendment, to which Your Honour has directed my attention, incorporates a principle which has been discussed this evening by two hon. members who have preceded me in the debate. That is the principle of using the resources in the first instance for the advantage of the Dominion of Canada itself. That is the principle I wish to discuss briefly. I must confess, in passing, that recent changes in government legislation, and changes in other minor things, including telephone books, where the word "dominion" has been dropped, have come as a shock to me. The word "dominion" is not nauseating, is it? Surely there is much to be said for the use of it; much can be said for the use *of old things.
We must deal with what was in the Dominion of Canada when it was a Dominion of Canada-and just what it is today, we do not know exactly. We do not know whether it is a commonwealth, whether it is just Canada, or what it is. I do not know. Does anyone else know? I would suppose that both the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Robinson) and Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) must take some responsibility for dealing with this pipe line situation. But the principle hon. members must keep in mind-
An all-Canada line.

There can be no question about it that the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) has greater ideas about Canada and Canada-first than any other member in the house. He, for one, will be the first to agree that Canada must be for Canadians, first. I am sure he would agree with that. There can be no doubt that he is the type of Canadian who would always exemplify in Canada the principle of Canada for Canadians.
How could we help agreeing with you?
I hope I am not aggravating hon. members.
They are just jealous.

I should like only to repeat some of the exhortations I have heard this evening, that Canada must be for Canadians, and that Canada must first be served. I can see no argument against it; what argument could there be? One must consider that there are 14 million people in the country-
There are 15 million now.
Well, what is 15 million people in a country like this today?
And they are nice people, too.

Hear, hear. And certainly the 325,000 mentioned a little while ago are good people. But we must look forward to a country in which we would have from 50 million to 100 million people. And if the country with that population is to be served by the resources of Canada, then one of the most important of those resources should be preserved for Canadians.
There is no one in the house who has a higher opinion of our neighbour to the south than I have. I believe the Americans are a fine people, and that we can share our natural wealth with them. But certainly we can share it with them only when we have made certain that our own needs are assured. When that is done, then I am sure that even those who hold strong opinions in this matter would be prepared to share with them. In this I have no doubt the hon. member for Simcoe East would agree. But he does not want to deprive Canadians of their God-given rights; I am sure he does not. That is the last thing in the world he would want to do. And knowing him as I do, I believe I can say safely-that it is nine o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: The committee was considering item 384.

Mr. Chairman, for the last forty-five minutes we have been discussing pipe lines, and associated matters. For a few moments I should like to discuss another matter of national importance, namely one of the national parks within my province. I refer to Elk Island national park, which is along the Yellowhead route, and which should have been developed rather than the one that is being developed. However, we will not argue about that at the moment.
During the last two years particularly we have had several thousand visitors at Elk Island park particularly on Sundays and holidays. Provision has been made for concerts at those times. Up to the present the concerts
Supply-Resources and Development have not cost the dominion government anything, but those in charge feel that, in the near future, because of the continuing importance of the park, it may be necessary to make some arrangements to pay small expenses, when voluntary performers cannot be obtained.
On March 12 last the president of the Alberta music board, Mr. Richard S. Eaton, wrote to the superintendent of the national parks service, Department of Resources and Development at Ottawa. Perhaps in explanation of the position I could not do better than to read three paragraphs from this letter. It reads as follows:
As you are doubtless aware, since the park has been developed to the extent that it may now be regarded as a summer resort available to many thousands of tourists each year, the facilities of the cultural activities branch of the department have been placed at the disposal of Dr. Love, superintendent, and on Sundays and holidays throughout the season, weather permitting, entertainment has been provided at no cost whatsoever to your department except perhaps bus transportation.
I might say that the Alberta music board has been set up under the cultural development act which is administered by the department of economic affairs at Edmonton. The letter continues:
Up to now, the detail involved in arranging for the entertainment Sunday after Sunday has been in the capable hands of Miss Audrey Ladler, the secretary of the branch, and whilst there is no suggestion of any change being made, we are of the opinion that the time is ripe for your department to enter into an official agreement whereby the cultural activities branch-for a consideration-undertakes to provide satisfactory entertainment whenever required at the park.
We feel that your estimates should contain an appropriation-the amount of which need not be very large-so that when the supply of volunteer entertainers runs out. Miss Ladler would be in a position to offer a small fee to ensure that each Sunday and holiday the public visiting the park is provided with a concert of some description. Whilst we are aware that in every community groups are to be found ready and willing to display their talent without remuneration, after a little while the person charged with the responsibility of making the arrangements finds that the source of supply has dried up and is unable to continue asking groups to do something for nothing.
Our suggestion is that you include in the budget for Elk island park a sum adequate to provide transportation, at least one meal, and a small donation, to each group asked to perform in the park. Should you accede to this request, we feel confident that the task of the person in charge of arrangements will be made much lighter, and the calibre of entertainment will be improved considerably. At the same time, the prestige of your department will undoubtedly be enhanced by the fact that you are providing patrons with an organized schedule.	.
During the past summer a male chorus from my home town of Vermilion put on a concert there one day, and a week from Sunday a ladies' choir from the same town is entertaining at the same park. I have read

Supply-Resources and Development of other groups in surrounding towns lying between the park and Edmonton, and some in other directions, having promised their support to the program. I feel that because of the importance of Elk Island national park at the present time, and the large number of local and outside people who are being entertained there every Sunday and holidays and other days during the week as well, the minister would be doing a service to Canada by acceding to the request in this letter.

I should like to ask the minister one or two questions about Riding Mountain national park. I have spoken about this matter before and have asked the minister to encourage larger camp sites there so that ordinary people can take advantage of them. The park is only about 150 miles from Winnipeg. It is an ideal situation for people from the whole area to come and spend a holiday at reasonable cost in these times of such high prices. I was not able to go there last year, but I intend to go this year. I was there two years ago. I had the idea from the minister in charge at that time that they intended to instal additional sewers and electric wiring along the lines of the camp site. I drew the minister's attention at that time to the fact that the use of coal oil lamps and other out-of-date lighting methods was very dangerous when so many people were visiting the camp sites. Would the minister tell me what extensions have been made there and what program is contemplated for this summer? Have you completed the highway through the park, running from Onanole through to Dauphin? Will you be able to accommodate more people this year than you could two years ago?

The electric wiring in Riding Mountain national park, to which the hon. member referred, is completed. It was completed last year. The road work to which he referred will be undertaken this year. There is quite a program of road construction in Riding Mountain national park. In reply to the last question as to whether or not we can accommodate more people in Riding Mountain this year than formerly, the answer is yes, we can.
How many more streets?
There are about 200 new lots.
Would the minister comment on the remarks I made a couple of minutes ago?

I might say the matter
brought to my attention by the hon. member is something I have discussed with the hon. member for Vegreville, and I have also had the representation to which the hon. member referred. We have of course put


the facilities of the camp at the disposal of this music association, such as a shell, and have tried to assist this voluntary effort, which is a very good one, in every possible way. We feel, however, that we cannot undertake to pay their expenses to and from the park, but nevertheless we will do everything we can with the facilities at our disposal to encourage this voluntary effort.

I think the minister did not
get my remarks correctly. I said the service was being rendered without any cost at the present time with the possible exception of bus transportation. The request made is, in the event that the supply of voluntary performers should run out, to enable those in charge of operating the program to ask somebody to come and be able to pay for their bus transportation, a meal, and possibly some donation.

I think it is some five
years ago now that I brought to the attention of the house and the then minister the fact that facilities in our national parks, and particularly in the parks at Banff and Jasper, were such that it required a fairly sizeable income to be able to go there to enjoy the parks. In other words, there was very little low-priced accommodation available. I made a strong plea at that time that some low-priced cabins should be erected. I think it was about two years later that some small move was made in this direction. Some buildings which had been used as army huts, or something of that sort, were moved into the park, and in that way a certain amount of low cost accommodation was provided. How far that has gone and how much low cost accommodation of that type there is in the parks I do not know. The first question I should like to ask the minister is what there is at the present time at Banff park particularly in the way of low-cost accommodation, cabins and so forth, where people with low incomes can afford to spend the night. I do not think the way in which this was done was particularly suitable, namely, the conversion of army huts. However, it was some help, though of course there was some complaint in Banff about the thing being done this way. I should like to impress upon the minister that a good deal more of this sort of thing should be done in our national parks. We should have cabins, which could be built at comparatively low cost, that would be in keeping with the natural surroundings. They could be built reasonably with these bark-sided boards; they would look quite all right and could be rented to people at low rates.

There is another side to this question of providing these facilities to people who are not wealthy. At the present time in Banff the building regulations are quite strict, so that it is impossible for people in the middle and lower income groups to build summer cottages or homes. The last list of lots of which I received a copy was dated May 25, 1950. The first ten or twelve listed give the legal description; the price of each lot is $650, and then the minimum value of the building to be constructed is given as $10,000. Mr. Chairman, the minister has been dealing with parks that are already in existence and the administration thereof, but I should like to ask a question or two with respect to a park which has been discussed but which has not yet been created. The minister will know that in the branch of his department which deals with this matter there has been considerable discussion about the Cape Blomidon site in Nova Scotia. Some two years ago before a committee in another place a definite promise was given that this park would be established.
The minister knows this location and I think he realizes the advantages of establishing a park there. The highest tides in the world are to be found in this area. Slightly to the west at Annapolis Royal there is the background of the earliest settlement in North America. There is the history of the expulsion of the Acadians and all the historical background incidental to that particular locality.
I should like to ask what is the policy of the department with respect to establishing a park there? Is it merely temporarily discontinued or will the minister reconsider establishing a park there some time in the immediate future?
In dealing with this matter perhaps I should state at the outset that I know of no statement by an official of the department to the effect that a national park would be established at Blomidon.
In another place.
By a departmental official?
Two years ago.

It did not come to my attention. At any rate, the matter of establishing a national park at Blomidon has been the subject of discussion, certainly in Nova Scotia, for a considerable time and has also been a matter of investigation. It is a matter in which I am considerably interested because I have spent some very pleasant hours at Blomidon looking over that magnificent scene and from where one can see a number of counties spreading out across the plain below.
The survey by the officials of the department reveals that the area in question does not conform to the standards laid down for national parks. Perhaps I should enumerate some of the salient requirements for a national park. They are as follows:
1.	The area should be representative of the most outstanding type of scenic lands in the province.
2.	The area should be of such a size as to provide a compact terrain adequately to support all forms of indigenous animals through all seasons and within the boundaries of the area.
3.	The area should provide features suitable for recreational development.
4.	It is preferable that the boundaries of the area conform to natural features such as height of land, rivers and shore lines.
5.	Should only embrace as far as possible lands in the natural state.
6.	Should not involve lands primarily suitable for agricultural use.
7.	Should not disturb present settlement which is self-supporting on the lands involved.
8.	Preferably lands still in the ownership of the crown.
9.	Accessibility to centres of population or highways of tourist travel.
10.	No excessive costs in construction of facilities required for the enjoyment of the public.
Dealing with the Cape Blomidon site on the basis of the above, it is an area unique in its natural formation but not entirely representative of the Nova Scotia seacoast and does not contain any other natural features such as inlets, lakes, streams or rolling hills as found typical of the general terrain of Nova Scotia. In so far as scenic attractiveness is concerned, it has only one feature of interest, its rugged precipitous shore line with views overlooking the sea and adjacent lands.

It is apparent from results of farming on lands now under cultivation that most of the land on the peninsula is productive. In the area under survey of about twenty-five square miles there are in the neighbourhood of 125 habitations in small communities such as Scotts Town and scattered farms, stores, schools, churches, sawmills, garages, service stations, etc. To include these lands in their entirety would result in considerable disturbance to people already established and apparently making a living.
To eliminate the lands now under cultivation from a possible park area would reduce land for consideration to about twelve square miles. This area would start from a sharp point at Cape Split and gradually widen at the eastern end at Borden Brook where the width would be approximately two miles. Such an area as described above would be of little use for preservation of wildlife in its natural state. Almost the entire coast line would be precipitous or bold rocky shore and, combined with the extremely high tides, would be of no use to the public for any form of recreation.
The conclusion that one must come to is that the area is not of the calibre usually considered for development as a national park inasmuch as the area is restrictive in size owing to the necessity of not disturbing lands now settled on and it has not the features for the usual all-round development for national parks.

There is another place I should like to mention particularly, and I suggest that the minister himself may have a natural reason for sharing my view as to the importance of that site. I refer to the Bell property at the end of Bras d'Or lakes. I am not referring to it simply because it was the home in, which Alexander Graham Bell lived during bis later years, and actually did carry out some of his last experiments. I am referring to it particularly because at that point is undoubtedly one of the greatest collections of experimental models to be found anywhere on this continent. That is a collection which would be a challenge to the mind of any young Canadian. There, in a wooden building, near the old Bell homestead, is collected a complete set of Bell experimental models, from which the telephone was patented. There are also the early models of the tetrahedral kites which were the forerunner of the first aircraft built anywhere in the British empire at that time. There is there also the actual aircraft which was first flown anywhere within what was then commonly described as the British empire. There is also there a collection of experimental models of air propellers of all types, which show the earliest experiments in that particular field.
There is also a collection of models of gramophones. It is a matter of great historic interest that Edison and Bell were working at the same time on the gramophone, and that Edison just happened to beat Bell out by a matter of a few days or

weeks. There are also models of an extremely interesting device invented by Bell, and which he described as a parafoil, to be used for the purpose of attacking submarines in the first world war. I do not believe they were ever used, but they did constitute an extremely important development and provided basic knowledge for some of the later devices employed in antisubmarine warfare.
I mention this to indicate some of the actual working models which are part of the history of scientific development in this country, and which are distinctly Canadian. I do suggest the time is long overdue for the taking of effective steps to house these extremely valuable models, which could never be replaced, in a fireproof building, so that they may be a centre of attraction and stand as a challenge to the imagination of young Canadians.
Although my association with the province of Nova Scotia is not as direct as that of the minister, I might say that I urged consideration of the project long before I came to this house, because to my mind it was one of the most inspiring and challenging experiences I have had to see collected there in one place this evidence of the great inventive genius which was brought to full development here in Canada.
I believe the minister would be doing something which would bring splendid results if he were to see that these were placed in a collection in a manner somewhat similar to what has been done at Dearborn, in connection with the Edison models, and with a view to having them reproduced in photographic form for distribution in all the schools. -

395. To provide for studies and surveys of the Red river basin in Canada, $182,000.

Would the minister tell us what has been done by way of work on the Red river. Is this being accomplished by the two governments, or only by ourselves? Is the American government co-operating with us in the work? I wonder if the minister

would tell us what is going on, so that the people in Winnipeg will know what is taking place.

A considerable amount of work has been undertaken by this department on its own direct account and in cooperation with other departments to accumulate data in the Red river valley, and the other streams and rivers that contributed to the disastrous flooding a year ago.
We have acquired a staff in Winnipeg under the direction of Mr. G. L. MacKenzie, who is on loan to us. He is chief engineer of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration. Temporary space was obtained in the district engineer's office at Winnipeg, and later permanent accommodation was obtained from the provincial government at 221 Osborne street north. Recruiting of staff proceeded as need arose, and at the present time Mr. MacKenzie has a staff under him of sixteen, all but three of whom are engineering or technical personnel.
The work initiated and virtually complete as at this date includes the hydrographic survey of the Red river from Winnipeg to the international boundary and north from Winnipeg to lake Winnipeg. Analysis of hydrometric and meteorological data, flood records, river slopes and aerial photographs was carried on concurrently. The assistance of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys was obtained to complete precise levelling operations, and this department also conducted surveys to develop the controls in the valley as a further step to contouring the area. The full co-operation of the greater Winnipeg dyking board, the Department of Public Works, the prairie farm rehabilitation administration and the United States geological survey has been obtained. In this connection Mr. MacKenzie and two members of his staff visited the corps of engineers office at St. Paul and were able to have very useful technical discussions so that the methods of carrying out hydraulic studies and other details would be correlated. At this conference it was determined that the improvement in the United States section of the basin would create no material change in the river regimen within the reasonable future.
The actual survey work has consisted in taking cross-sections of the river generally at 1,000-foot intervals with lesser intervals being used at some of the sharp bends. Extra sections were taken above and below all bridges. These cross-sections consist of taking soundings in the river at 20-foot intervals and the topography of the banks for a distance of 100 to 500 feet beyond the top of the
Supply-Resources and Development banks on both sides of the river. Information is also being obtained as to the nature of the bed of the river by means of probings. Certain cross-section information between Emerson and Morris was already available in the office of the district engineer, water resources division, at Winnipeg.
Information was secured regarding the hydraulic gradient of both the Red and Assiniboine rivers for various stages of water during this spring. Staff gauges were accordingly placed by Mr. MacKenzie's staff throughout the Red river from Emerson to lake Winnipeg and up the Assiniboine river to Headingly. The P.F.R.A. also established a number of gauges on the Assiniboine river from Headingly upstream.
Once the necessary surveys are complete, maps will be drawn on a scale of 600 feet to 1 inch with an accompanying profile on a horizontal scale of 1,000 feet to 1 inch, and most of the work during the coming year will consist in the preparation of plans and profiles from the information which has been gathered. The maintenance of one or two survey parties throughout most of the summer will be necessary to obtain additional data as the need for this information arises. Office studies will include investigation of possible river channel improvements, protective works, flood diversion schemes, storage or retardation possibilities, hydraulic elements and determinations of costs and benefits of various schemes or combinations of schemes. The prairie farm rehabilitation administration will be doing most of the survey work on the Assiniboine river. The dyking board has completed the Assiniboine river surveys within the city of Winnipeg. I think the danger is over for this spring.
I thank the minister for his explanation.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
